change.title: pr-80329-flat
change.author: Cristian Sotomayor

findings.title: Debug logging left in at Error level, including every batch's full ID list
findings.body: Each batch callback logs twice with `r.log.Error`: once before the delete (534, 554, 576) and once after (537, 557, 579). The first call also includes the whole `ids` slice. That slice holds up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` IDs, and the new test sets that to 32767. `untilDoneOrCancelled` (643-660) always runs one last batch that returns 0, so these Error lines fire on every cleanup cycle even when there is nothing to delete. That covers MaxAge and MaxCount for each annotation type, plus the tag cleanup. Together with the ticker going down to 1 minute in `cleanup.go:77`, this puts a steady stream of false error-level logs into production logs and alerting. The `"err", err` field at 534/554/576 is always nil because the error was checked just above. Remove these lines, or lower them to Debug and log only counts.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker cut from 10 minutes to 1 minute; looks like a leftover from debugging
findings.body: This ticker drives all eight cleanup jobs (lines 96-105), not only annotations: tmp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs and query history. Every Grafana instance would now run all of them 10× as often. The per-run timeout is still `9 * time.Minute` (line 89), which was sized to fit inside the 10-minute interval and no longer matches. Nothing in the PR description explains the change. Restore `time.Minute * 10`, or make the interval a config setting and keep the timeout in line with it.

findings.title: Building the inline ID list with repeated Sprintf is quadratic
findings.body: `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` copies the whole growing string on every iteration. This path only runs when the batch size is above 999, so the batch can hold tens of thousands of IDs (the test uses 32767), and that is O(n²) copying per batch. Use a `strings.Builder` with `strconv.AppendInt`, or `strings.Join` over the formatted IDs.

findings.title: "running the max count delete again" no longer runs anything again
findings.body: Each subtest now creates its own data (line 116) and wipes the tables afterwards (120-127). This case therefore just inserts 9 annotations (3 per type) and checks that MaxCount=3 deletes nothing. The name still describes the old behaviour, where it ran a second time over the previous case's leftover state. That idempotence check is gone. Rename the case, or run `cleaner.Run` twice in one subtest so it still tests a second run.

contracts.action: CleanAnnotations / CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags now fetch IDs in one session, then DELETE ... WHERE id IN (ids) in a separate session
contracts.equivalent_path: Previous single-statement DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (subquery LIMIT n) a) run through executeUntilDoneOrCancelled
contracts.before_after: Before: one atomic statement per batch. After: SELECT the IDs, then DELETE by primary key. The IDs come from autoincrement keys. An annotation's `created` timestamp and its rank by id only move it further toward deletion as new rows arrive, so the fetched IDs still meet the criteria at delete time. If a row was already removed, the delete just affects 0 rows for it. The loop stops when a batch affects 0 rows, so if every fetched ID had been deleted concurrently, cleanup stops early and picks up again on the next cycle, as the comment at 523-525 says.
contracts.visible_effect: Old or excess annotations and orphaned tags get removed in the background; users never see a result directly. Every batch writes Error-level logs (reported as a finding).
contracts.failure_mode: If fetch or delete fails, the error propagates through untilDoneOrCancelled (652-654) to the cleanup job. cleanUpOldAnnotations logs it unless it is DeadlineExceeded. Nothing is journaled, so nothing is lost; the next tick retries.

contracts.action: SQLite path inlines the IDs into the DELETE statement when the batch size is over 999
contracts.before_after: The IDs are int64 values read back from the database and formatted with %d, so the statement cannot be injected into. The batch-size check guarantees len(ids) <= batch size, so the placeholder path never goes above 999 parameters on SQLite.

contracts.action: Cleanup ticker interval changed to 1 minute
contracts.equivalent_path: Run loop with the 9-minute per-run timeout in clean()
contracts.before_after: Runs are synchronous, so they cannot overlap; a slow run just causes ticks to be dropped. All eight jobs now run 10× as often (reported as a finding).
contracts.visible_effect: More DB load and more log volume on every instance.

contracts.action: Test fixture inserts annotations with explicit IDs via InsertMulti
contracts.before_after: xorm InsertMulti includes autoincrement columns when their value is non-zero, so the tag rows' annotation_id values match the inserted annotation IDs.

summary: The new fetch-then-delete-by-ID cleanup is logically sound: the deletes stay within the fetched IDs and failures propagate. But two pieces of debug leftover should be reverted before merge. Every batch writes Error-level logs that include the full ID list, even when nothing is deleted. And the global cleanup ticker drops from 10 minutes to 1, which runs all eight cleanup jobs 10× as often, while the 9-minute timeout stays the same. Two smaller points: the inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation, and one test name is now misleading.
